questions.explain: The chapter states plainly that RDS for SQL Server has no read replicas, so a readable-secondary scale-out topology requires full-control platforms like EC2, Azure VMs, or GCE.
options: Create RDS read replicas of the SQL Server instance
Use the RDS Proxy read/write splitting endpoint
Not available on RDS — this topology requires EC2/Azure VMs/GCE
Enable the 'readable secondary' parameter on the RDS instance
questions.q: According to Chapter 21, how do you get readable secondaries for read scale-out on Amazon RDS for SQL Server?

questions.explain: ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly in the connection string routes reporting traffic to readable asynchronous AG secondaries while OLTP stays on the primary.
options: It routes read traffic to async AG secondaries, leaving OLTP on the primary
It forces all connections to the primary replica
It enables synchronous commit mode for the session
It disables read locks on the primary
questions.q: What does ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly do in the Chapter 21 scale-out topology?

questions.explain: The chapter's rule is that the distributor belongs on a dedicated instance for busy topologies — never co-locate it with a struggling publisher.
options: On the publisher, to keep latency to zero
On a dedicated instance — never co-located with a struggling publisher
On the subscriber, to balance the load
Inside a managed service, to avoid VM cost
questions.q: Where should the distributor live in a busy transactional replication topology?

questions.explain: Distributed AGs must not be used for sharding or write-scaling a single logical dataset, because SQL Server has no built-in conflict resolver worth relying on.
options: DR with a runnable secondary site
Geographic read locality from each site's primary
Controlled cutovers during migrations
Write-scaling a single logical dataset (sharding across AGs)
questions.q: Distributed availability groups are legitimate for DR, geographic reads, and migrations — but NOT for which use case?

questions.explain: Sync replication makes every commit wait for the network round trip — single-digit ms within a region, tens to hundreds of ms across regions — which throttles write throughput, so sync replicas stay within one region.
options: Synchronous replication doubles write throughput cross-region
Sync replicas must stay within one region; async is for cross-region, because each commit waits on the network round trip
Async replication guarantees zero data loss on failover
Cross-region latency has no effect on commit times
questions.q: What is the Chapter 21 rule about synchronous replication and distance?

title: Chapter 21: Distributed SQL Server: Replication and Scale-Out Topologies
